Hi Eduarda, it's James. Good news: Mark accepted the hundred and five as a starting point, so NorthPack starts due diligence on Monday. They will have two weeks in the data room, and then a full day of meetings with Victor and Paul. Their team is good, and they will dig into three areas: the contracts with the big customers, the pension plan for the employees, and any litigation. Please sit down with Paul before Monday and ask him every difficult question that you can think of. If there is a problem, we want to hear about it first. Thanks.

In due diligence, the quality of your questions decides the quality of your information. Start with open questions, with what, how and why, so that the other person explains instead of just saying yes or no. Then use follow-up questions to dig into the details. Be careful with direct questions about sensitive topics. Is there a problem with your accounts? can sound like an accusation. Could you walk me through how you prepare your accounts? gets the same information, and the other person stays relaxed. Finally, never accept a vague answer. If someone tells you it's not a big deal, ask them how much it is in dollars.

NorthPack accepted one hundred and five million as a starting point for due diligence. Before the data room opened, Eduarda sat down with Paul, the CFO. She asked him whether Lane had any litigation. Paul explained that a former supplier was asking for two million dollars. Eduarda wanted to know why the case wasn't in the last audit. They agreed to put a clear disclosure in the data room.
